title: Draupadi's secret was no charm
hookLine: Krishna's wife asks Draupadi for a love charm, and Draupadi answers with the householder's real work
last: THE FIRE IS THE WITNESS OF TRUTH KEPT HER DHARMA EVEN AS A CAPTIVE.

lines: AN ANSWER WITH NO MAGIC IN IT.
cards: The question is a little rude, and the guest asks it anyway. The Pandavas are living in the forest, and Krishna comes to visit with his wife Satyabhama. While the men talk, the two women sit together.
Satyabhama leans in. Your husbands are heroes, she says, in paraphrase, and they never cross you. How do you do it?
Is it a vow? A mantra? Some herb, some charm?
Tell me, so Krishna will be like that with me. Draupadi could laugh, or be offended. Instead she gives a long answer, with no magic in it at all.

teach.h: CHARMS ARE A ROAD TO RUIN
teach.b: Draupadi starts by refusing the premise. Charms and potions, she says in the epic's Forest Book, are a road to ruin.
A husband who learns his wife is working spells on him grows afraid of her, the way a person fears a snake in the house.

teach.h: A DAY'S WORK, NOT A SPELL
teach.b: Then she tells Satyabhama what she actually does, and it reads like a day's work. She sets her pride aside. She rises before the household and sleeps after it.
She sees that guests are fed and the servants looked after. Then a line some readers stop on: back at Indraprastha, the brothers left the household's income and spending to her.
She alone kept track of it. The woman remembered from the dice hall was also the one who knew where the kingdom's money went. Here's the teaching.
Hinduism names four stages of life: student, householder, forest-dweller, renunciant.
The householder, the grihastha, isn't the lesser one.

The law book of Manu says that as every creature lives by the air, the other stages live by the householder: the house feeds the student, the guest, the wandering monk. So the work Draupadi lists isn't beneath dharma.
It is dharma, done daily. Readers still argue over the speech. Some hear devotion, some a capable queen, some are uneasy with an ideal built around serving.
And she says it all in exile, with no palace left, from memory, without complaint.

how: Hindus meet Draupadi in retellings of the Mahabharata, in storytelling and theater, and in some regions as a goddess with her own temples and festivals; her conversation with Satyabhama is read in many ways, from a model of devotion to a portrait of a capable queen.

o: a queen who keeps her husbands close with spells
the queen whose secret is the householder's daily work
a princess who never had to run a household

p: asks for a vow, a mantra or a charm

s: Draupadi tells Satyabhama about a secret mantra
she refuses the idea of charms and describes her daily work instead.
Draupadi says she alone kept track of the household's income and spending
back at Indraprastha, she says, the brothers left that burden to her.
in Hindu teaching, the householder's stage is the lowest of the four
Manu says the other stages live by the householder, as creatures live by the air.

games.q: a friend says someone who runs a home all day isn't doing anything spiritual. by Draupadi's answer, what fits?
o: in Hindu teaching, the householder's work is dharma; the other stages lean on it.
true. only monks and priests do spiritual work.
it's spiritual only if a mantra is said over it.
games.why: Draupadi swapped Satyabhama's charm for a day's work, down to the accounts. grihastha, the householder's life, is one of the four stages, and Manu calls it the one that feeds the rest.

practice: Bring to mind one ordinary day in your home, or a home you grew up in, and ask who kept it running: the food, the bills, the guests, the small repairs. Hindus call that work grihastha dharma, the householder's path.
Let one person come to mind, maybe you, and let each breath out thank them silently for it. If you pray, you can name them before God.

wordCard.voice: Draupadi. Asked for a charm, she described the householder's work, down to a kingdom's accounts. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Draupadi, Drupada's daughter. the epic also calls her Panchali, the princess of Panchala.

carryVoice: Your line: the householder's work is dharma. Draupadi's secret was never a charm. Until tomorrow.
